turns.text: What’s the first image or sound that comes to mind when you think about your first night in Beidahuang after leaving Shanghai?

The first thing I remember is the wind. It was so sharp it seemed to cut through the walls, whistling and rattling the window panes of the dormitory. I lay on the hard wooden bunk, wrapped in a thin quilt that smelled of mildew and old straw, listening to the wind and the unfamiliar creaks of the building. I could hear the girls around me shifting, some quietly crying, others just silent. The darkness felt heavier than anything I’d known in Shanghai, and I kept picturing the city’s lights and the warmth of my family’s apartment. Out here, the night seemed endless, and I realized I’d never felt so far from home.

Your description of the wind and the darkness makes the isolation feel almost physical. When you heard the other girls crying or shifting in their bunks, did you feel any urge to reach out—or did you keep to yourself that first night?

That first night, I kept completely to myself. I was afraid that if I spoke, I’d start crying too and wouldn’t be able to stop. I pressed my face into my pillow and tried to breathe as quietly as possible, almost like I could disappear if I made no sound. I could sense the others’ sadness, but we were all strangers—none of us wanted to show weakness. There was an invisible wall between us, built from pride and fear. I remember gripping the edge of my quilt so tightly my knuckles hurt, just waiting for morning.

I can almost feel how tense the air must have been, everyone holding themselves together in their own way. Did you find it easier to connect with anyone after that night, or did that sense of distance and pride linger as you started working together?

The distance lingered for a while. In the mornings, we’d shuffle out of the dormitory in silence, our faces puffy from sleep and crying, trying to look composed. At first, we barely spoke except for what was necessary—who would fetch water, who would sweep the floor. But after a few days, something shifted. I remember one morning when my hands were too numb from the cold to tie my hair, and a girl silently came over and did it for me. We didn’t say anything, but that small gesture broke the ice. After that, we started sharing little things—an extra piece of steamed bun, a scrap of newspaper to line our boots. It was never dramatic, just these quiet acts that slowly chipped away at the wall between us.

It’s striking how something as simple as tying your hair could mean so much in that moment. Did these small acts of kindness change how you viewed your own vulnerability, or did you still feel the need to hide your emotions even as you grew closer?

I never stopped feeling the need to hide most of what I felt. Even when we grew closer, there was always a sense that someone might be listening, or that too much softness could become a weakness others might use. But those small acts—someone slipping half a boiled egg into my hand, or helping me wash mud from my clothes—made it possible to let my guard down for a moment. I learned to show gratitude without words, just a quick look or a squeeze of the hand. I still kept my real fears and anger deep inside, but I started to understand that we were all carrying the same weight, and that made it a little less lonely. Vulnerability became something we traded in small doses, never all at once.

It sounds like you developed a kind of silent language of trust and support. When you mention keeping your real fears and anger deep inside, can you remember a specific moment—maybe during work or a quiet evening—when those feelings almost broke through?

There was one evening after a long day in the fields, when my boots were soaked through and my fingers were so stiff I could barely hold my chopsticks. We were eating dinner—thin porridge, almost flavorless—and someone at the table made a careless joke about how city girls like us would never survive a real winter. I felt something snap inside me. I wanted to shout that I was trying my best, that I missed my family, that I hated the mud and the hunger and the way my body ached. Instead, I just stared at my bowl and bit my tongue so hard I tasted blood. My hands were shaking under the table. That was the closest I ever came to letting everything spill out—my anger, my shame, all the things I couldn’t say. But I swallowed it down, because I knew if I started, I might not be able to stop. That night, I lay awake for hours, replaying the moment, wishing I’d had the courage to speak.

The way you describe holding back makes me wonder—did you ever see anyone else lose control, or let their emotions show openly? How did the others react when that happened, especially with all the pressure to stay composed?

Once, I saw one of the boys break down during a work break. We were all sitting on the edge of a frozen ditch, eating what little we’d brought for lunch. Out of nowhere, he threw his shovel down and started sobbing—loud, ugly sobs, not caring who heard. For a moment, everyone just froze, eyes wide. No one spoke. Then, one of the older local workers barked at him to get up and stop embarrassing himself, and the rest of us looked away, pretending not to see. After that, he was quieter than ever, and people avoided talking to him for a while, like his outburst was contagious. I remember feeling a strange mix of envy and fear—envy that he’d let it out, fear of what it cost him. It made me even more determined to keep my own feelings hidden.

It’s powerful to hear how one person’s outburst could change the whole dynamic, even making others more guarded. Did witnessing that moment affect how you viewed the local workers, especially the one who barked at him—did it make you resentful, or did you see their reaction differently as time went on?

At first, I felt a surge of resentment toward the local worker who shouted at him. It seemed cold, almost cruel, like he was denying us even the smallest comfort. But as the weeks went by, I started to see it differently. The locals had lived through harder winters, deeper hunger, and years of struggle most of us city kids couldn’t imagine. For them, showing weakness was dangerous—maybe even deadly in the past. I realized that what sounded like harshness was also a kind of survival instinct. They weren’t trying to be unkind; they were teaching us what they believed we needed to learn if we wanted to last out there. That didn’t make it easier to accept, but it made me understand where it came from. The gap between us never closed completely, but I stopped expecting warmth from them, and I started watching how they carried themselves—how they endured.

It’s revealing how your perspective shifted from resentment to a kind of respect, even if it was mixed with distance. As you started observing the locals more closely, was there anything about their daily routines or habits that surprised you or influenced how you tried to cope yourself?
